Yesterday you finished the analysis. Today you finish the notebook, and then you tell eleven other
teams what you found.

The whole morning is yours to finish in. Presentations are in the afternoon for that reason. The
one thing the morning is not for is new analysis: if you find yourself computing something you have
not computed before, you are adding scope on the last morning, and the answer is almost always to
stop.

The notebook is due when you push it, before you go to lunch.

## The morning: what "finished" looks like

Work through these in order, because each one is worth more than the one after it. If you run out
of morning, having done the first three properly beats having started all five:

1. **Restart the kernel and run every cell from the top.** Do this first, not last. A notebook that
   only runs in the order you happened to write it is a notebook that will fail in front of the
   class.
2. **Step 10, Visualize.** One figure that carries the claim. Axis labels with units, a title that
   states the finding rather than naming the variables, and a legend if you used `hue=`.
3. **A markdown cell under every one of the ten headings.** Where a step was genuinely not needed,
   the cell says so in a sentence. An empty heading is the only thing here that reads as unfinished.
4. **The claim, near the top.** Two or three sentences: what you asked, what you found, and what
   the finding rests on. Somebody who reads only that and looks at your figure should understand
   the project.
5. **Delete the wreckage.** Every project accumulates cells that were a good idea on Thursday.
   Remove them. Your notebook is easier to present when it contains only the path you took.

The full description of the deliverable is on the [final project page](final_project.qmd).

## Handing it in

The notebook is due when you push it, **before lunch on Friday**. Leave yourself the last fifteen
minutes of the morning for it, because this is the step that goes wrong under time pressure. There
is nothing to submit after class.

1. Put the project notebook in its **own repository**, not in your coursework repository.
2. **Keep the outputs.** This is the one place where the advice in the
   [GitHub session](interactive-sessions/8a_github.qmd) does not apply: `nbstripout` removes
   figures and printed output from every commit, which is right for coursework and wrong for a
   notebook whose figures are the point. Do not configure `nbstripout` on this repository.
3. Add a one-paragraph `README.md` naming the team, the dataset, its source URL, and the question.
4. Push, then open the repository in a browser and confirm the notebook renders with its figures
   showing. GitHub renders `.ipynb` files directly, so this takes ten seconds and catches the
   problem while you can still fix it.
5. Send me the repository URL.

::: {.callout-tip title="If git is fighting you at five to twelve"}
Do not lose the notebook to a merge conflict on the last morning. Download the `.ipynb` from
Positron, email it to me, and sort the repository out afterwards. The work is the thing that
matters; the repository is how it travels.
:::

## The presentations

**Twelve minutes per team, then three for questions.** I will keep time and I will be strict about
it, because the last team of the afternoon deserves the same twelve minutes as the first.

Present **from your notebook**, not from slides. Scroll through it and talk. You have already
written the structure, and rebuilding it in Google Slides on Friday morning is work that teaches
you nothing.

A twelve-minute walkthrough that works, every time:

| Minutes | What |
|---------|------|
| 0 to 2  | The dataset. Where it came from, what one row is, how many rows, and why you chose it. |
| 2 to 4  | The question, and the two you set aside. |
| 4 to 7  | What the data needed before it could answer it. Cleaning, filtering, transforming, and anything surprising. |
| 7 to 10 | The figure. Talk the class through the axes before you talk about the finding. |
| 10 to 12 | The claim, what it rests on, and what you would do with another week. |
: {.hover .bordered tbl-colwidths="[20,80]"}

Both members present. On a team of three, one can drive the notebook while the other two talk.

::: {.callout-note title="Things worth saying out loud"}
The most interesting minute in most of these presentations is the one where a team says what went
wrong. A column that turned out to be text, a grouping that produced a group of one, a question
the data could not answer. Say those things. Everybody else hit the same wall and thinks they were
the only one.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Two things to avoid"}
- **Do not say "significant".** You have not been taught a hypothesis test and you are not
  expected to have run one. Say a difference is large or small, and show the counts it rests on.
- **Do not apologise for your project.** Every project in this room was built in two days by people
  who learned pandas eight days ago. Present what you found.
:::

## After the last presentation

That is the course. You arrived on the 31st, and in nine days you have imported, explored, cleaned,
filtered, sorted, transformed, grouped, aggregated, joined, reshaped and visualised real data, and
then done all of it again on a dataset nobody chose for you.

Everything on this site stays where it is. The cheatsheets in particular are written to be returned
to, and you will return to them.
